name: ACE
listed_description: An OO Network Programming Toolkit in C++.
reason: No numeric comparison reachable. The ACE_TAO repo page and ACE/performance-tests/README only list benchmark programs (Synch-Benchmarks, TTCP with C sockets versus ACE wrappers, UDP, Misc) with no committed results; ACE/apps/JAWS is an ACE-based web server. The only comparative claim found is directional, from WebSearch snippets of the Hu, Pyarali and Schmidt JAWS papers (a USENIX NT 1997 paper and the Schmidt-site PDF globalinternet.pdf): JAWS 'consistently outperforms existing Web servers, such as Apache, Java Server, PHTTPD, Zeus, and Netscape Enterprise' over 155 Mbps ATM on a dual-CPU 180 MHz UltraSPARC 2. The papers themselves (usenix.org, dre.vanderbilt.edu, ftp.icm.edu.pl) are EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so no numbers could be read; the listed project page https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/ACE.html is also blocked. Lead for a session with paper access: retrieve the JAWS paper and record JAWS (ACE) versus Apache/Zeus as a tier B entry (peer-reviewed, 1997 hardware).

name: AGENT++
listed_description: C++ framework provides a complete tri-lingual SNMP v1/2c/3 protocol engine and dispatcher for the development of SNMP agents.
reason: No numeric comparison found. agentpp.com is EGRESS_BLOCKED, github.com/agentpp shows no public repositories, and a WebSearch for AGENT++ benchmarks against net-snmp returned only package listings (Buildroot, Fedora copr, AUR) that describe features (SNMPv1/v2c/v3 engine, Apache-2.0 licence) with no performance claims.

name: asnlc (asn1c, Lev Walkin)
listed_description: Compiler of ASN.1 specifications into C source code.
reason: No claim that asn1c is faster than anything. The repo README (BSD-2-Clause, 1.2k stars) has no performance statements, and lionet.info is EGRESS_BLOCKED. The only numeric comparison reachable is third-party and shows asn1c slowest: eerimoq/asn1tools examples/benchmarks/c_source README encodes and decodes one PDU 1,000,000 times (UPER): asn1tools 1.229 s at -O3 and 2.987 s at -Os, asn1scc 4.023 s and 6.166 s, asn1c 10.902 s and 12.569 s; asn1c executable text 63733 bytes versus 5553 (asn1tools) and 12073 (asn1scc), and asn1c uses dynamic memory and supports all codecs. The list's guessed category (http-servers-frameworks, baseline standard HTTP server) is wrong; the project is an ASN.1 codec generator (serialization-and-formats). The similarly named Objective Systems ASN1C benchmark pages (obj-sys.com) are for a different, commercial product.

name: Boost.Beast
listed_description: HTTP and WebSocket built on Boost.Asio in C++11.
reason: No numeric comparison against websocketpp or any other library. The Beast FAQ (doc/qbk/08_design/4_faq.qbk) answers 'You need benchmarks!' with: 'The energy invested in Beast went into the design of the interfaces, not performance', and says only that a small program compares Beast's parser to the NodeJS reference parser (test/bench/parser/bench_parser.cpp) and others compare Beast's dynamic buffers to Asio's; no results are committed. The websocketpp comparison page (doc/qbk/08_design/3_websocket_zaphoyd.qbk) is design-only (type requirements, shared_ptr use, type erasure). The README states performance as a goal ('thousands of connections') with no numbers. A WebSearch for Beast versus websocketpp benchmarks found nothing numeric; the rippled commit message that introduced basic_parser (git.inftf.org) may hold parser numbers but is EGRESS_BLOCKED.

name: Boost.Interprocess
listed_description: Header-only Boost library that supports kernel-level shared memory and memory-mapped files, with in-built synchronization mechanisms
reason: No numeric comparison against any baseline. The repo's only benchmark (bench/bench_offset_ptr.cpp) times offset_ptr operations relative to raw pointers (a cost ratio, not a win) and commits no results; the documentation section 'Performance of Boost.Interprocess' (doc/interprocess.qbk) is qualitative advice on allocations and named objects; release notes for 1.93 only say 'Improved the performance of several offset_ptr's operations' and 'Optimized spin-based synchronization' with no numbers. Guessed category (websocket-grpc-rpc) is wrong; the project is shared-memory IPC.

name: Breep
listed_description: Event based, high-level C++14 peer-to-peer library.
reason: No numeric comparison against any baseline. README (EUPL-1.1, 146 stars) only says serialization adds a fixed 64 bits of overhead versus raw bytes (TCP header 320 bits) and that the library is 'very, very slow to compile with'; there is no benchmark directory or shootout entry.
